evidence_set: PubMed and Scopus searched from market introduction (gabapentin 1997, pregabalin 2004) to 31 March 2017, with reference lists; both authors screened independently; 106 articles included (Figure 1). The framework weighs rewarding effects, ICD-10 dependence criteria in clinical studies and case reports, relapse, treatment seeking, social harm and overdose toxicity, and, as the authors' stated hypothesis, takes behavioural dependence in people with no earlier history of substance use as the best sign of a drug's own power to cause dependence.

250 former prisoners living in a correctional community centre in Pittsburgh (written questionnaire): 16% (41) reported having misused gabapentin in the past; gabapentin abuse was endorsed by 26% of the 145 with opioid use disorder against 4% of the 105 without it (p < 0.0001); 1 of 30 people with cocaine use disorder and no opioid use disorder reported abusing gabapentin; every participant had at least one further substance use disorder.

Nine register studies (Finland, Sweden, Germany, the UK, European pharmacovigilance) all pointed to rising deaths involving gabapentinoids, mainly pregabalin, nearly always with other drugs, mostly opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol and antidepressants. US poison-centre annual reports: fatality records involving a gabapentinoid 38 of 2,576 (1.5%) in 2012, 41 of 2,113 (1.9%) in 2013, 41 of 1,408 (2.9%) in 2014 and 59 of 1,371 (4.3%) in 2015; pregabalin-related deaths always with other medicines; in each of 2013-2015 one record (0.05-0.07% of all fatality records), always gabapentin, attributed to a gabapentinoid alone, with no information on blood levels or autopsy. The authors sum up that pure overdoses appeared relatively safe but can become lethal in mixtures, mostly with opioids and sedatives.

evidence_set: The authors suggest that fentanyl, which accumulates in fat with repeated use and can take weeks to clear, can be displaced by buprenorphine, and that this may contribute to withdrawal within 48 hours of fentanyl use even with conventional starting procedures; they hypothesize that severe withdrawal after methadone may reflect poorly managed withdrawal from too little opioid effect early in treatment, because first outpatient doses are capped and methadone takes more than a week to reach steady levels. The Conclusions say that people who take buprenorphine within 24 to 48 hours of fentanyl are at significantly greater risk of severe withdrawal than those who wait more than 48 hours, a comparison the model did not make (the paper names no reference group; by the editors' reconstruction it was the 1 week-1 month group).

evidence_set: Scoping review by authors from a university department of biomedical sciences and public health in Ancona and an institute of emerging health professions in Philadelphia, partly funded by the Italian government's Department of Antidrug Policy: 31 designer benzodiazepines considered; PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar and Web of Science searched to March 2021, with agency reports; references reviewed for relevance by one author; included were reports in which a designer benzodiazepine was the sole or explicit contributory cause of poisoning, driving impairment or death; of 372 potentially relevant reports, 324 were excluded and 49 included, on 12 drugs; 254 cases reported 2008-2021: 1 drug offence, 2 self-administration studies, 3 outpatient admissions, 44 emergency-department admissions, 63 DUID and 141 deaths, tabulated in Table 1. Most patients and decedents were young, of both sexes, often with a history of substance use and mental illness; cases came from Finland, Germany, Japan, Norway, Poland, Sweden, the UK and the USA. The included reports are not appraised.

Emergency cases as the drug-by-drug text describes them: clonazolam, primary adverse effect CNS depression (two of six not confirmed, amounts self-reported); diclazepam, 2 of 3 in a severe state of agitation and disorientation with stimulants and dissociatives also detected, the third with CNS depression and a withdrawal syndrome; etizolam, three children drowsy and wobbly after eating coloured pills thought to be sweets (confirmed in one) and a man found unconscious next to a syringe of heroin; flualprazolam, seven young people after a benzodiazepine thought to be alprazolam, three sedated with verbal impairment, two with CNS depression and two without symptoms, flualprazolam not confirmed in three; flubromazepam, four in profound agitation and delirium followed by rigidity and CNS depression; flubromazolam, 18 in a severe state of CNS depression with functional and motor impairment, the sole drug detected in 16. Flubromazolam was identified in Sweden in 10 seized white tablets labelled 'XANAX' and reported to the EMCDDA in October 2014.

Few pharmacokinetic studies exist, so concentrations are currently hard to relate to effects; diclazepam, etizolam and phenazepam blood concentrations overlapped in impaired and non-impaired drivers, and etizolam and flualprazolam concentrations were similar in DUID cases and deaths (the authors suggest differences in tolerance); because polypharmacy is the rule, causation often cannot be assigned to a single drug; many people exposed may never develop significant adverse events (citing Carpenter et al.); many cases go undetected for lack of analytical methods or awareness; the newest drugs may cross-react with common benzodiazepine immunoassays, which often cannot tell designer from prescribed benzodiazepines; how pathologists and toxicologists attribute the role of these drugs in deaths is largely unknown.
